'''''Vaccinium angustifolium''''', commonly known as the '''wild lowbush blueberry''' and the '''low sweet berry'''<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |title=About Maine Wild Blueberry |url=https://extension.umaine.edu/blueberries/about/ |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries |language=en-US|via=the [[University of Maine]]}}</ref> is a species of [[blueberry]] native to eastern and central [[Canada]], [[Great Lakes]] and the [[northeastern United States]].

==Description==
[[File:Pinus banksiana forest.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|''V. angustifolium'' growing in a forest of another fire-adapted species, ''[[Pinus banksiana]]'']]

''Vaccinium angustifolium'' is a low spreading [[deciduous]] shrub growing {{convert|5 to 60|cm|frac=2}} tall.<ref name=":0">{{FEIS |genus=Vaccinium |species=angustifolium |type=shrub |last=Tirmenstein |first=D. A. |date=1991}}</ref> Its [[rhizome]]s can lie dormant up to 100 years, sprouting when given the adequate amount of sunlight, soil moisture, and oxygen content.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} The [[leaves]] are glossy blue-green in summer, turning a variety of reds in the fall. The leaf shape is broad to elliptical, with the [[bud]]s brownish red in stem [[axil]]s.

The [[flower]]s are white or pink,<ref name=":03">{{Cite web |title=About Maine Wild Blueberry - Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries - University of Maine Cooperative Extension |url=https://extension.umaine.edu/blueberries/about/ |access-date=2022-11-30 |website=Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries |language=en-US}}</ref> bell-shaped, {{convert|4 to 6|mm|2|frac=8}} long.<ref name=eFloras>{{eFloras|1|250065717|Vaccinium angustifolium |family=Ericaceae |first=Sam P. |last=Vander Kloet}}</ref> The [[fruit]] is a small sweet dark blue to black berry, full of [[antioxidant]]s and [[flavonoid]]s.

Several buds may be on a healthy stem, and each bud can open up and have several blossoms. A blueberry field that has full plant coverage can have as many as 150 million blossoms per acre.{{citation needed|date=January 2025}}

Chromosome number is 2n = 48.<ref name="y832">{{cite journal | last=Redpath | first=Lauren E. | last2=Aryal | first2=Rishi | last3=Lynch | first3=Nathan | last4=Spencer | first4=Jessica A. | last5=Hulse-Kemp | first5=Amanda M. | last6=Ballington | first6=James R. | last7=Green | first7=Jaimie | last8=Bassil | first8=Nahla | last9=Hummer | first9=Kim | last10=Ranney | first10=Thomas | last11=Ashrafi | first11=Hamid | title=Nuclear DNA contents and ploidy levels of North American Vaccinium species and interspecific hybrids | journal=Scientia Horticulturae | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=297 | year=2022 | issn=0304-4238 | doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2022.110955 | article-number=110955| doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Etymology ==
The [[species epithet]] ''angustifolium'' is a combination of the Latin words {{wikt-lang|la|angustum}} meaning 'narrow', and {{wikt-lang|la|folium}} meaning 'leaf'.{{cn|date=March 2026}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
The lowbush blueberry is native to central and eastern [[Canada]] (from [[Manitoba]] to [[Newfoundland]]) as well as north-central and eastern United States<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vaccinium angustifolium Aiton {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:858831-1 |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> (growing as far south as the [[Great Smoky Mountains]] and west to the [[Great Lakes]] region).<ref>{{PLANTS|symbol=VAAN|taxon=Vaccinium angustifolium|access-date=2013-08-04}}</ref><ref>{{BONAP|ref|genus=Vaccinium|species=angustifolium}}</ref> In its native habitat the plant grows in open conifer woods, old fields, and sandy or rocky balds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=vaan |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref>

Glacier ice from the [[Last Glacial Period|Ice Age]] sculpted the [[Maine]] landscape and is responsible for creating some of the most productive ''V. angustifolium'' habitats.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Geological History and Climate Change {{!}} Wild Blueberry Heritage Center |url=https://wildblueberryheritagecenter.org/geological-history-and-climate-change/ |access-date=2022-11-30 |language=en-US}}</ref> The species is [[fire-tolerant]], and its numbers often increase in an area following a forest fire.{{citation needed|date=January 2025}}

This plant grows best in wooded areas, old abandoned farmyards or open areas with well-drained [[acidic soil]]s. In some areas it produces natural blueberry barrens, where it is practically the only species covering large areas.<ref name=eFloras />

== Ecology ==
Many animals feed on the fruit and foliage of the lowbush berry, some of which include [[American black bear|black bears]], [[raccoon]]s, [[fox]]es, [[white-tailed deer]] and [[bird]]s.<ref name=":0" />

Its leaves are also popular among caterpillars. It is a larval host to the [[pale tiger moth]], the [[peppered moth]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bugguide.net/node/view/19107|title=Species Biston betularia - Pepper & Salt Geometer - Hodges#6640|website=bugguide.net}}</ref> the [[chain-dotted geometer]], the [[saw-wing moth]], the [[blueberry gray moth]], the [[mousy angle moth]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bugguide.net/node/view/554947|title=Species Macaria argillacearia - Mousy Angle Moth - Hodges#6282|website=bugguide.net}}</ref> ''[[Caloptilia vacciniella]]'', [[Andromeda underwing]], the [[Drasteria adumbrata|shadowy arches]], the [[Eueretagrotis perattentus|two-spot dart]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bugguide.net/node/view/22844|title=Species Eueretagrotis perattentus - Two-spot Dart Moth - Hodges#11008|website=bugguide.net}}</ref> the [[Feltia jaculifera|dingy cutworm moth]], the [[Lacanobia subjuncta|speckled cutworm]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bugguide.net/node/view/43460|title=Species Lacanobia subjuncta - Speckled Cutworm - Hodges#10299|website=bugguide.net}}</ref> the [[Pangrapta decoralis|decorated owlet]], the [[Syngrapha epigaea|pirate looper]], [[Xestia normaniana|Norman's dart]], the [[Xylena cineritia|gray swordgrass moth]], the [[pink-edged sulphur]] butterfly, the [[pawpaw sphinx]] moth, and the [[blueberry leaftier moth]].

== Cultivation ==
''Vaccinium angustifolium'' has a two-year production cycle.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Two-Year Wild Blueberry Production Cycle - Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries - University of Maine Cooperative Extension |url=https://extension.umaine.edu/blueberries/factsheets/production/wild-blueberry-2-year-production-cycle/ |access-date=2022-11-30 |website=Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries |language=en-US}}</ref> The first year is known as the vegetative year and the second is known as the fruit-bearing year. 

In order to be productive each year, most farmers divide their land to have half their crop in the vegetative year while the other half is in the fruit-bearing year.<ref name=":05">{{Cite web |title=About Maine Wild Blueberry - Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries - University of Maine Cooperative Extension |url=https://extension.umaine.edu/blueberries/about/ |access-date=2022-11-30 |website=Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries |language=en-US}}</ref>

Traditionally, blueberry growers burn their fields every few years to eliminate shrubs and fertilize the soil. In [[Acadian French]], a blueberry field is known as a {{lang|fr|brûlis}} (from {{lang|fr|brûlé}} 'burnt') because of that technique, which is still in use.{{citation needed|date=October 2024}}

=== Pruning ===
[[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] regularly burned away trees and shrubs in parts of eastern Maine to stimulate blueberry production. Modern farmers use various methods of burning or mowing to accomplish this.<ref>{{cite web |date=1914-06-30 |title=The University of Maine - Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries - 229-Pruning Lowbush Blueberry Fields |url=https://umaine.edu/blueberries/factsheets/production/pruning-lowbush-blueberry-fields/ |access-date=2013-08-04 |publisher=Umaine.edu}}</ref> There are several methods growers use to stimulate blueberry production on their land, such as burning the land or using a [[flail mower]], [[brush hog]], lawnmower, etc. to cut the plants off as close to the ground as possible without scalping the land. These procedures are used to promote the spreading of rhizomes under the soil. Some growers use a [[sickle mower]] in the fall after the crop has been harvested to mow the plants off, leaving about 1–2 inches of stem so the growers can burn the remainder of the plants in the spring, using less fuel for the fire.

Farmers then treat their crops with pesticides to control weeds and insects.<ref name=":52">{{Cite web |title=Two-Year Wild Blueberry Production Cycle - Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries - University of Maine Cooperative Extension |url=https://extension.umaine.edu/blueberries/factsheets/production/wild-blueberry-2-year-production-cycle/ |access-date=2022-11-30 |website=Cooperative Extension: Maine Wild Blueberries |language=en-US}}</ref> The fields are then left for new growth to emerge, develop, and flourish for the remainder of the year.

=== Pollination ===
During the harvest or fruit bearing year, blueberry growers rent [[honey bee]] hives to put in their fields for pollination. These hives are placed in the fields at a density range of anywhere from 1–8 hives per acre. The hives are placed in the fields at 10–20% bloom allowing the bees to have enough forage rather than going elsewhere to forage. Hives are left in blueberry fields for 2 weeks on average, allowing the bees to pollinate the variety of clones in the field, all of which bloom at different times during the two-week period.

Some growers also use [[bumblebee]]s as well in ambitions of maximum pollination. Bumblebees will fly in colder and wetter weather conditions than the honey bee will, and they also pollinate in a different way than the honey bee. Bumblebees can sonicate the flowers, which releases pollen from deep inside the [[Dehiscence (botany)|poricidal]] anthers. This is known as [[buzz pollination]].

Blueberry growers also rely on many wild bees for pollination, including [[solitary bees]] like ''[[Andrena carlini]]'' and ''[[Colletes inaequalis]].''<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bushmann|first1=Sara L.|last2=Drummond|first2=Francis A.|date=August 2015|title=Abundance and Diversity of Wild Bees (Hymenoptera: Apoidea) Found in Lowbush Blueberry Growing Regions of Downeast Maine|journal=Environmental Entomology|volume=44|issue=4|pages=975–989|doi=10.1093/ee/nvv082|issn=1938-2936|pmid=26314043|s2cid=23922592}}</ref>

== In culture ==
The wild lowbush blueberry is the Nova Scotian Provincial Berry.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Heritage |first=Canadian |date=2017-08-15 |title=Nova Scotia |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/provincial-territorial-symbols-canada/nova-scotia.html |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref> [[Oxford, Nova Scotia]], is nicknamed the "Wild Blueberry Capital of Canada".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Orkin |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YX7zDQAAQBAJ |title=Nova Scotia |date=2017-03-05 |publisher=Bradt Travel Guides |page=289 |isbn=978-1-78477-040-2 |language=en}}</ref>

It is also the [[state fruit]] of Maine.<ref>{{Cite web |title=State Berry - Wild Blueberry |url=https://www.maine.gov/sos/kids/about/symbols/berry |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=www.maine.gov}}</ref> Maine's state dessert is [[blueberry pie]] made with wild blueberries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=State Dessert - Blueberry Pie |url=https://www.maine.gov/sos/kids/about/symbols/dessert |access-date=2022-12-01 |website=www.maine.gov}}</ref>
